newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul pledges further reform as it joins OECD.
newsitem.headline: Seoul pledges further reform as it joins OECD.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Thursday pledged further economic reforms as the booming Asian nation became the 29th member of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Devemopment (OECD).

In comments to coincide with South Korea's formal accession to the Paris-based club of rich nations at 1100 GMT, when it deposited membership documents with the French government, Kim hailed the move as a coming-of-age.

South Korea will "push policies of reform to raise the nation's regulations to the level of advanced nations and undertake institutional reforms for further liberalisation," Kim told ambassadors from OECD member nations in Seoul.
"The membership is very significant, not only for the glory of the Korean people, but also for other OECD member nations who share the values of democracy and a free market economy."
"The Republic of Korea has grown from ruins to become one the 10 largest economies of the world in just one generation."
South Korea will be the second Asian member after Japan and the first from the region's newly industrialised economies.

Seoul was invited to join the OECD on October 11. Opposition parties had threatened to block ratification in parliment, saying the OECD could force Korea to open its markets to foreign competition too quickly.

Separately, a government statement said membership reflected South Korea's new status in the world and its moves to become It "reflects the appreciation of the world community for the remarkable feat achieved by the ROK people in economic development as well as their attainment of a mature level of democratisation", the statement said.
Critics have said rapid liberalisation could deal a blow to the economy, which is staggering under the weight of widening current account deficit.
The Bank of Korea, the central bank, said the deficit would reach $22 billion this year because of a slump in exports, compared with a shortfall of $8.95 billion in 1995.

An export slump resulting from plunging international prices of key commodities is forecast to slash the nation's gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 6.4 percent in 1997, down from an estimated growth of 6.9 percent this year and 9.0 percent in 1995.
Since applying for OECD membership in March 1995, South Korea has accelerated the opening of its financial markets to foreign investors.
